data.summary:
Input: Two strings text1 and text2.
Output: An integer representing the length of their longest common subsequence.
Rules: A subsequence is formed by deleting some or no characters without changing the relative order of the remaining characters.
constraints: text1 and text2 consist of only lowercase English characters.

data.generator_code:
import random

def generate(rng, n):
    alphabet = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'
    s1 = ''.join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(n))
    s2 = ''.join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(n))
    return [s1, s2]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    s1 = 'a' * n
    s2 = 'b' * n
    return [s1, s2]

data.key_insight: We can build a 2D table where dp[i][j] stores the length of the longest common subsequence of text1[0...i-1] and text2[0...j-1]. If characters match, we take 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]. Otherwise, we take the maximum of excluding the current character from either text1 or text2.

steps.title: Initialize DP table
steps.detail: Create a 2D array dp with dimensions (len(text1) + 1) by (len(text2) + 1) initialized to zeros.

steps.title: Fill the table
steps.detail: Iterate through each character of text1 and text2, updating dp[i][j] based on whether text1[i-1] equals text2[j-1].

steps.title: Return result
steps.detail: The bottom-right cell dp[len(text1)][len(text2)] contains the length of the longest common subsequence.

data.pattern_summary: Dynamic programming breaks a problem down into overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem only once and storing the results in a table or memo.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. The problem asks for an optimal value and contains overlapping recursive branches where the same index pairs are visited multiple times.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers work well when traversing a single sequence or inward from both ends, but matching subsequences requires exploring multiple branching deletion choices.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding windows are used for contiguous subarrays or substrings, whereas subsequences do not need to be contiguous.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A greedy choice at each step does not guarantee the globally longest common subsequence because local matches can lead to suboptimal outcomes later.

signals.phrase: length of their longest common subsequence
signals.hint: Points to an optimization problem where we want to maximize a count.

signals.phrase: deleting some or no characters without changing the relative order
signals.hint: Implies multiple recursive branching choices at every character position.

data.brute_force_idea: Use recursion to explore all possible choices: if characters match, increment the count and move both indices forward; if they do not match, branch by advancing one index at a time and take the maximum result.
data.brute_force_why: At each step where characters do not match, the function branches into two recursive calls, leading to an exponential number of calls.
data.bottleneck: The recursive function recomputes the answer for the same pairs of indices (i, j) many times over different branches.
bottleneck_hints: Trace the recursive calls for small strings with repeated characters.
Notice how many times the function is called with the exact same arguments i and j.
Consider storing the results of subproblems so you never solve the same pair of indices twice.

data.overview: The algorithm finds the length of the longest common subsequence between two strings using dynamic programming. It builds a 2D table where each entry represents the optimal solution for prefixes of both strings.
data.intuition: Imagine comparing two words letter by letter using a grid. If the current letters match, you extend the best common path found so far diagonally. If they don't match, you take the best result from either dropping a letter from the first word or the second word.

pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when mapping 1-based table indices to 0-based string indices.
Forgetting to size the DP table with dimensions (m + 1) and (n + 1).
Confusing substrings (contiguous) with subsequences (not necessarily contiguous).

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach recomputes overlapping subproblems exponentially. By storing the results of each state in a 2D table, the dynamic programming solution ensures each pair of indices is processed exactly once, transforming exponential repetition into a systematic grid traversal.

derivation.note: Allocates a 2D grid of size (m + 1) by (n + 1).
The outer loop iterates m times.
The inner loop runs n times for every iteration of the outer loop.
Performs constant time comparison and table lookups per inner iteration.

data.time_summary: Lines 5 and 6 create a nested loop running m times n total executions, matching the measured evidence where line 6 and its inner operations scale quadratically with input size. Thus, the total time complexity is O(m * n).
data.space_summary: The algorithm allocates a 2D array dp of dimensions (m + 1) by (n + 1) to store intermediate subproblem results, resulting in O(m * n) space complexity.
data.takeaway: When a recursive problem revisits the same index states repeatedly, replace recursion with a 2D table that builds solutions iteratively from base cases up to the target inputs.
mistakes: Off-by-one errors when sizing the dp table, failing to account for the zero-length base case rows and columns.
Confusing string index i and j with table index offsets when checking text characters against the dp grid.
Iterating loops up to m and n instead of m + 1 and n + 1, missing the boundary conditions.
